item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Hegseth defends against impeachment push
item.description:
The US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is defending against a push from within his own party to impeach him.

You'll hear from someone who knows a thing or two about impeachment proceedings - former federal Watergate prosecutor Nick Ackerman.

Then, Qantas is cutting more than 800 positions from the airline in coming years.

And we'll dive into the government's plans to introduce mandatory artificial intelligence safety and security standards for developers.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: A Premier's plea to fix the age care crisis
item.description:
The aged care system is in crisis and at breaking point: that's what South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas will argue at a rally in Adelaide today.

He's urging the federal government to take immediate action.

Then, the US tech giant Nvidia has opened an independent investigation following reports that its chief executive had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Meanwhile, the COP-31 climate talks are underway in Türkiye, with Australia leading negotiations on new agreements to reduce global emissions.

And we hear from an award-winning photojournalist who's been covering the war and humanitarian crisis in Sudan.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Was Nvidia's CEO targetted by a Chinese spy?
item.description:
Technology giant Nvidia says it will investigate a report CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Mr Huang has admitted to staff he had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Carrington Clarke breaks down a story rocking the tech sector.

Then, the government backs down over its plans to sell key defence sites, now allowing four to remain in public hands.

And New Zealanders have had their say over who should lead the country, but it's going to take some time to figure out exactly what they said.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: David Jones suppliers scrambling
item.description:
"They're a pain in the arse to work with," says one David Jones supplier who's grappling with the department store's announcement its going into voluntary administration.

Renniks Group boss Michael Pitt says he doesn't expect David Jones to pay the $16,000 it owes his company, nor cover the $40,000 worth of merchandise and packaging he has sitting in his warehouse. 

We also hear from the union representing retail workers as it plans to up activity to protect staff. 

Then Democrats want to roll back the Trump administrations tariffs, so what impact could the midterms have on gobal trade?

And we'll cross the pond as New Zealand heads to the polls this weekend.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Blue-nami sweeps US mid-terms
item.description:
The Democrats have seized control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives following the midterm elections.

We're gonna wrap the big races, hear from a pollster, a former Australian Ambassador to the US, and a Congressman-elect, who flipped a Republican seat blue - completely out out of the blue.

We'll also look at how Republicans are assessing the loss, with the President now admitting the war with Iran may have had something to do with it.

And there's a telling market reaction too that is worth looking at with Carrington Clarke.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: The 5th rate rise this year
item.description:
The Reserve Bank has hiked interest rates for a fifth time this year, taking the rate to an 18-year high.

The RBA has updated its economic forecasts - revealing it doesn't expect inflation to return to its target band of 2-3% until late next year.

We hear from the Finance Minister and the Shadow Treasurer. 

Then we cross to the US as voters have their say in the mid-term elections.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Why is a Democrat endorsing a Republican in Michigan?
item.description:
In Michigan, a shock last-minute endorsement may have tightened the midterm race. 

Sitting Democrat congresswoman Haley Stevens has publicly backing Republican candidate Mike Rogers over her party's own nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.

We also turn to the race in Texas, where a Democrat is threatening the Republican's hold on the state. 

Then over in the Carribean, Prime minister Anthony Albanese is going to raise Australia's recent changes to visa rules for backpackers with the British Prime Minister.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Gun buyback scheme begins in NSW
item.description:
Some license holders in New South Wales will be able to surrender their guns from today.

It's part of the state government's response to the Bondi Beach massacre last year, including limiting the number of guns a person can own and the introduction of stronger background checks.

Then, the Nationals Senate leader Bridget McKenzie has been a vocal opponent of the caps on the number of guns people can own - she shares her response to the scheme. 

And overseas, Caribbean activists want the United Kingdom to confront its role in transatlantic enslavement, which saw more than 10 million Africans stolen from their homes from the 15th to 19th centuries.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: An Ambassador's emotional plea at the UN
item.description:
A moment at the United Nations has reminded the world of the ongoing crisis in Myanmar. We hear from the country's Ambassador who was brought to tears with a plea, stopping dignitaries in their tracks. 

Then, outrage, anger and questions mount in Spain following the country's second deadly high speed rail disaster this year.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Spain grapples with another deadly train tragedy
item.description:
We head to central Spain with a reporter who's been on the ground of the worst rail disaster in Europe since 2013. 

He tells us survivors are frustrated at repeated rail-incident deaths, and the disaster could play a role in the upcoming Spanish election. 

Then, there's still a stalemate in the Israeli election and the question many are asking; could the surging Arab-Israeli parties end up the kingmakers?

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: What next for Israel?
item.description:
The Israeli elections are too close to call as counting continues.

Neither the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party, nor its main rival bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party is on track for a majority in the 120-seat parliament. 

We hear from a former Israeli diplomat on what the country can expect over coming weeks. 

Then, the Australian Prime Minister is being accused by the opposition of misleading parliament over a grant to a golf club in his electorate

The Communications and Sport Minister Anika Wells will answer Sally's questions over the 6 million dollar grant.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: How Brazil's Lula won from behind
item.description:
The left-wing incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has come from behind to win the Brazilian election in extraordinary fashion. 

But the right wing challenger, son of the former president Flavio Bolsonaro hasn't yet conceded defeat. 

So what on earth is happening in Brazil?

Then some Labor politicians are trialling the use of an AI tool to identify and hide abusive and threatening comments on social media. We hear from the Minister for Women who's used the tool herself.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Parliament in solidarity with Helen Haines
item.description:
Federal parliament will sit today for the first time since independent MP Dr. Helen Haines was attacked outside her electorate office.

Parliamentary business will be suspended, with the prime minister to move a motion expressing support for Ms Haines and her family.

She remains in hospital in a serious but stable condition.

Then - Brazilians have been voting in a hugely consequential election that could take the country down two very different paths. We cross to Sao Paulo as polls close.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: The $25b energy project causing a political headache
item.description:
A major review into Australia's biggest renewable energy project has found Snowy Hydro 2.0 could cost up to $25 billion, with the completion date pushed out another year.

The project had an initial budget of $2-billion dollars and was originally expected to start operating in 2021.

It's now it's expected to not be fully operational until 2029. 

We hear from the government, the opposition and the project's CEO. 

Then, 12 months ago we spoke to Dr Saya Aziz - an Australian anaesthetist working in Gaza, who described horrific scenes of mass casualties, medical equipment shortages, even a lack of soap - along with the constant fear of air strikes. She comes back on the show after returning from her second trip to Gaza.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Why are house prices falling?
item.description:
House prices have fallen in all capital cities for the first time in 15 years - that's according to new data from listings company Domain.

Prices across the capitals fell 4.7% in the September quarter - wiping almost $60,000 off the median price of a home.

We hear from the Federal Housing Minister Claire O'Neill. 

Then, we'll turn to the Greens,  and party leader David Shoebridge's message on our show that he expects Jordon Steele-John to take leave from the party.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: How can we better protect politicians?
item.description:
Politicians are raising security fears of their own, in the wake of an attack on prominent independent MP Dr helen Haines.

So how can we better protect the people representing us?

Then, One Nation leader Senator Pauline Hanson apologises for a cartoon mocking Senator Jacqui Lambie's health struggles after she suffers vaginal prolapse.

You'll hear from One Nation deputy leader Barnaby Joyce.

And we''ll also cross to Canada to find out about an effort to split the country.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Australia rocked by attack on Dr Helen Haines
item.description:
How are representatives across the political spectrum digesting news of an attack on an Australian politician?

Today's episode of the Breakfast Wrap hears from the bystander who intervened in Wangaratta, the town's Mayor, as well as independent federal politicians, the government and the opposition, the House Speaker and historical context from Michelle Grattan.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Thousands arrested in French unrest
item.description:
Thousands of pepole have been arrested across France following days of chaotic unrest.

We'll take you to the streets of Paris and we'll hear how the French President is responding.

Then, where is the line for political satire? 

Independent Senator Jacqui Lambie thinks One Nation has  crossed it, with its latest video that mocks her health battle after she publicly revealed that she suffered vaginal prolapse.
